title: External Remote Services
summary: External Remote Services describes adversary use of legitimate remote access services to gain an initial foothold or to re-enter an environment from outside the perimeter. The services involved are ones the organisation exposes deliberately for business reasons: virtual private network concentrators, remote desktop gateways, remote shell and file transfer services, and hosted remote management or desktop-as-a-service platforms. Because the service is expected to be reachable and the protocol itself is legitimate, the technique sits on the boundary between initial access and persistence, and identical session types appear in both contexts. At a mechanism level an adversary authenticates with credentials obtained elsewhere, uses a valid account issued to a contractor or third party, exploits or misconfigures the gateway itself, or registers an account with a cloud-hosted remote access platform that the organisation cannot see at all. The telemetry lives mainly in the gateway and identity layers: authentication records with source address, client and device attributes, session start and duration, concurrent session anomalies, and configuration changes to the service, after which endpoint records show what the session did once established. Investigations separate legitimate remote work from abuse by examining the source network and its reputation, whether the account was expected to use that client and that geography, whether the session coincided with password spraying or credential stuffing activity, and whether the same account performed administrative actions outside its normal pattern. Strong controls tie every exposed service to multifactor authentication and device posture rather than treating network reachability as sufficient proof of identity, and they log enough session context to reconstruct who connected from where and when.
objectives: Inventory externally reachable remote access services and identify which are business-essential.
Read gateway authentication and session logs to establish source, client and duration for a session.
Correlate a remote session with identity anomalies and with post-authentication endpoint activity.
Evaluate multifactor, device posture and session recording controls for each remote access path.
Explain how third-party and hosted remote management platforms complicate visibility and attribution.
Write detection logic for remote sessions from unexpected geographies or concurrent with credential attacks.
